problem: The lead says the cost is one message per entry when every process is busy. That contradicts the chapter's own formula C = (N − 1) + 1 = N: with N processes each entry costs N messages, not one. The comparison also switches units, pitting 'per entry' for this algorithm against 'per process' for reply-based schemes.
fix: Say: with N processes all busy, one entry costs N messages, made up of N − 1 REQUEST broadcasts plus one token transfer, against 2(N − 1) messages per entry for Ricart–Agrawala.

problem: The chapter never states the rule that fills Q, and the trace in step 3 uses a rule the algorithm does not have. A holder that is not requesting and receives REQUEST(2,1) with RN[2] = LN[2] + 1 must send the token to P2 at once, so Q is never [2,4,3]. Requests enter Q only when the holder is inside the critical section and cannot forward immediately, or when the token is in transit.
fix: Add the missing rule to Section 2: on receiving REQUEST(j, sn) while holding the token, set RN[j] = max(RN[j], sn); if the holder is not inside the critical section and RN[j] = LN[j] + 1, send the token to j immediately, otherwise append j to Q. Then correct step 3: P1 forwards the token to P2 on the first request with Q empty; P2 queues P4 only because that request arrives while P2 is inside the critical section, and P2 sends the token to P4 on exit. The entry order P2, P4, P3 and the 12-message total stay the same; the queue values do not.

problem: It is false that a duplicate token never serves a process twice for the same request number. Suppose i requests with RN[i] = 1 and the good copy grants it, so that copy holds LN[i] = 1. The stale copy still holds LN[i] = 0. When the stale copy reaches i, RN[i] = 1 = LN[i] + 1 passes the test and i enters again for the same request.
fix: State that after a crash duplicates the token, mutual exclusion can break in two ways: two different processes may hold a copy and enter together, and the same process may be granted twice, because a stale copy carries an out-of-date LN that still passes the entry test. The copy with the larger LN is the one to keep; the other must be destroyed, for example by a token sequence number.

problem: The answer repeats the same wrong claim: 'The LN inside each copy still prevents a second grant to the same process for the same request number.' A stale copy with a smaller LN[i] will pass the test RN[i] = LN[i] + 1 for a request already granted by the other copy.
fix: Answer: two holders can pass their tests and enter together, so mutual exclusion is lost; the same process can also be granted twice from a stale copy, because its LN is behind. Nothing inside the token limits the damage on its own; one of the two tokens must be detected and removed before either is used again.

problem: The conclusion is right but the reason is wrong. RN[i] = 7 does not imply LN[i] = 7; if the request numbered 7 has not been granted yet, LN[i] is still 6 or less. The answer teaches a false fact about the two arrays.
fix: Answer: max keeps RN[i] = 7, so the delayed REQUEST(i, 5) changes no state and is ignored. It is safe because the entry test always works from the highest request number seen, so an older number can neither create an extra entry nor push LN[i] backwards; grants only move LN[i] forward, one request number at a time.

problem: The chapter says the token 'also travels with the holder's copy of RN' and Q1 counts RN as token state. In the standard algorithm the token is only the pair (Q, LN); RN stays at each process. Travelling copies of RN add nothing, and a receiver that overwrote its own RN with them could lose a request that reached it but not the sender.
fix: Say the token carries Q and LN[1..N], and every process keeps its own RN[1..N]. Change Q1's answer to the two token fields, Q and LN, noting that RN is a per-process array, not part of the token.

where: Section 1 versus Section 2 and Exam trap 1
problem: Section 1 and trap 1 say LN is written by the process that has 'just finished' or 'just used' the token, but step 2 correctly sets LN[i] = RN[i] before entering the critical section. A student may write LN at exit instead of at entry.
fix: Use one wording everywhere: process i sets LN[i] = RN[i] as part of taking the token and before entering the critical section, and only the process that has been granted a request ever writes its own LN entry.
